Two thoughts in the piece stuck out for me. The first was,

In other words, it is like the accusation of witchcraft. Something negative is observed, and it is assumed that a dark and vague force is responsible. There is no conceivable evidence which could disprove the allegation, and none is needed to support it beyond the fact of the unpleasant reality observed.

This seems to be a mindset all people are quick to assume. It honestly sounds like the anti-vaxxer groups; blame the thing that is quickest and easiest even if it isn't correct at all. The second is his ending. The idea that a perfectly capable person would allow for their own demise because of perceived wrongdoing tied to an unknowable evil is the exact point we are at now.

:-/

Here's the rub: a dramatic work like Arthur Miller's "The Crucible" does relate to the "Red Scare" and "superstitions", "the zealot mindset" and intangible charges. Why? Because it happens in a social sphere. They're both courtroom dramas. "The Witch" happens in isolation.

There's no commentary on "larger society" because there's no society outside of a family. In Romero movies, the survivors represent a cross-section of society. In "The Witch", you have one family -- in which the traditional roles of family members are most important. There's no courtroom, no evidence, no "what other people think" -- just parents and children. There is no attempt to communicate evidence or convince others.

In the point about a "perfectly capable person would allow for their own demise because of perceived wrongdoing tied to an unknowable evil", I struggle to identify the demise or the perceivers of wrong-doing in "The Witch". The movie had an opportunity to explore these themes at the beginning, but the very limited courtroom scene served more as exposition than inciting action.

The author may be right in his philosophy. I'm not debating that. But finding this message in the movie is indicative of an obsession. The same review could equally relate to "The Thing".
